text: A 'deep fake' is defined as AI-generated or manipulated image, audio, or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities, or events [1]. This content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful [1].

'AI literacy' means the skills, knowledge, and understanding that enable providers, deployers, and affected persons to make an informed deployment of AI systems [1]. This understanding must take into account their respective rights and obligations within the context of the Regulation [1]. It also involves gaining awareness regarding the opportunities and potential risks that AI can cause [1].
A 'small mid-cap enterprise' or 'SMC' is defined as a small mid-cap enterprise as defined in point (2) of the Annex to Recommendation (EU) 2025/1099 [1].

A "substantial modification" is a change to an AI system after it has been placed on the market or put into service that was not foreseen or planned in the initial conformity assessment by the provider [1]. This change must affect the AI system's compliance with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2, or result in a modification to the intended purpose for which the AI system was assessed [1]. If a distributor, importer, deployer, or other third party makes such a modification to a high-risk AI system, they are considered a provider and are subject to the provider's obligations [3](b). However, changes to a high-risk AI system and its performance that were pre-determined by the provider at the time of the initial conformity assessment and are part of the technical documentation shall not be considered a substantial modification if the system continues to learn after being placed on the market or put into service [2].

The 'AI Office' is the Commission’s function responsible for contributing to the implementation, monitoring and supervision of AI systems and general-purpose AI models, and AI governance, as specified in the Commission Decision of 24 January 2024 [1]. The Commission shall develop Union expertise and capabilities in the field of AI through the AI Office [3]. The AI Office may invite all providers of general-purpose AI models, along with relevant national competent authorities, to participate in creating codes of practice [4].

This Regulation does not apply to AI systems where and in so far they are placed on the market, put into service, or used with or without modification exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [1]. Furthermore, it does not apply to AI systems which are not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, where the output is used in the Union exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities [1].

AI systems released under free and open-source licences are not exempt from the regulation in all cases [1]. The obligation set out in Article 53, paragraph 1, points (a) and (b), does not apply to providers of AI models released under a free and open-source licence that allows for access, usage, modification, and distribution, and whose parameters are publicly available, unless the general-purpose AI models present systemic risks [3]. Similarly, the obligation set out in Article 54, paragraph 6, does not apply to providers of general-purpose AI models released under a free and open-source licence that allows for access, usage, modification, and distribution, and whose parameters are publicly available, unless the general-purpose AI models present systemic risks [2]. Furthermore, the Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences if they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50 [1]. However, this exception does not apply to third parties making accessible to the public tools, services, processes, or components, other than general-purpose AI models, under a free and open-source licence when they are used or integrated in a high-risk AI system [4].

AI systems or AI models, including their output, specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development are not covered by this Regulation [1]. Furthermore, this Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service, although testing in real world conditions is not covered by that exclusion [2]. However, a 'general-purpose AI model' definition excludes AI models that are used for research, development or prototyping activities before they are placed on the market [3].

Yes, the AI Act applies to providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union [4]. This applies to importers and distributors of AI systems as well [4].

Providers and deployers of AI systems must take measures to support the development of AI literacy of their staff and other persons dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf [1]. These measures must consider the technical knowledge, experience, education and training of the staff, as well as the context in which the AI systems are to be used and the persons or groups on whom the AI systems are to be used [1]. This obligation does not require providers or deployers to guarantee any specific level of AI literacy for any individual [1]. Furthermore, codes of conduct can promote AI literacy, particularly for those involved in the development, operation, and use of AI [4].

Natural persons assigned human oversight must be enabled to properly understand the relevant capacities and limitations of the high-risk AI system and monitor its operation, including detecting and addressing anomalies, dysfunctions, and unexpected performance [2][4](a). They must also remain aware of the possible tendency to automatically rely or over-rely on the output of the high-risk AI system, especially when it provides information or recommendations for decisions [2][4](b). Furthermore, they must be able to correctly interpret the high-risk AI system’s output using available interpretation tools and methods [2][4](c). Overseeing natural persons must have the ability to decide not to use the high-risk AI system or to disregard, override, or reverse its output in any specific situation [2][4](d). They must also be able to intervene in the system's operation or interrupt it using a 'stop' button or a similar procedure to bring the system to a safe state [2][4](e).

The provider must keep the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the national competent authorities for 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [1][4]. Furthermore, the provider must keep the EU declaration of conformity at the disposal of the national competent authorities for a period ending 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service [4].

The provider or, where applicable, the authorised representative must register themselves and their high-risk AI system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service, unless the system is one of the exceptions listed in point 2 of Annex III [1]. Furthermore, if a provider determines that an AI system is not high-risk according to Article 6(3), that provider or the authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database before placing it on the market or putting it into service [2].

As an employer, you must inform workers' representatives and the affected workers that a high-risk AI system will be used at the workplace before it is put into service or used [1]. This information must be provided according to the rules and procedures established in Union and national law and practice regarding worker information and their representatives [1]. High-risk AI systems in employment include those used for recruitment, selection, analyzing or filtering job applications, and evaluating candidates [2][4](a). They also include systems used to make decisions affecting work-related relationships, promotion, termination, task allocation based on individual traits, or monitoring and evaluating performance and behavior [2][4](b).

Deployers must perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2) [5]. This obligation applies to deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III [5]. The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 applies to the first use of the high-risk AI system [1].

For a fundamental rights impact assessment, deployers must perform an assessment consisting of several elements [3][4]. These elements include identifying the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by the system's use in the specific context [4]. Furthermore, the assessment must detail the measures to be taken if those risks materialize, including arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms [3]. If a data protection impact assessment under Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 is already conducted, the deployer may include cross-references to or relevant parts of that assessment [1]. The AI Office will develop a template, potentially with an automated tool, to help deployers comply with these obligations [2].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems listed in Annex III that make decisions or assist in making decisions related to natural persons must inform those natural persons that they are subject to the use of the high-risk AI system [1]. For high-risk AI systems used for law enforcement purposes, Article 13 of Directive (EU) 2016/680 shall apply [1]. Furthermore, any affected person subject to a decision taken by the deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, which produces legal effects or significantly affects that person's health, safety, or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations from the deployer regarding the AI system's role in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision [4].

A provider who considers that an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk must document its assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service [1]. Such a provider is subject to the registration obligation set out in Article 49(2) [1]. The provider must also be able to provide the documentation of the assessment upon request from national competent authorities [1]. If a market surveillance authority finds that the AI system is high-risk during evaluation, it will require the provider to take all necessary actions to bring the AI system into compliance with the Regulation's requirements and obligations [2]. If the provider fails to bring the AI system into compliance within the prescribed period, it will be subject to fines according to Article 99 [3].

SMEs, including start-ups, may comply with certain elements of the quality management system required by Article 17 in a simplified manner, provided they do not have partner enterprises or linked enterprises within the meaning of Recommendation 2003/361/EC [1]. The Commission is tasked with developing guidelines on the elements of the quality management system that can be complied with in a simplified manner, while ensuring the level of protection is not affected or the need for compliance with requirements for high-risk AI systems is diminished [1]. An SME is defined as a micro, small or medium-sized enterprise as defined in Article 2 of the Annex to Recommendation 2003/361/EC [2].

The use of AI systems to infer emotions of a natural person in workplace institutions is prohibited, unless the AI system is intended for medical or safety reasons [1]. An 'emotion recognition system' is defined as an AI system used to identify or infer the emotions or intentions of natural persons based on their biometric data [3]. If an employer uses a high-risk AI system at the workplace, the employer who is the deployer must inform workers’ representatives and the affected workers about the use of that system [2]. Furthermore, deployers of an emotion recognition system must inform the natural persons exposed to it about the system's operation and process personal data according to specific Regulations and Directives, unless the system is permitted by law for detecting, preventing, or investigating criminal offenses [4].

The use of AI systems for the evaluation or classification of natural persons or groups of persons over a certain period of time based on their social behaviour or known, inferred or predicted personal or personality characteristics, where the social score leads to detrimental or unfavourable treatment in social contexts unrelated to the data's original collection, is prohibited [1]. This prohibition also covers detrimental or unfavourable treatment that is unjustified or disproportionate to the social behaviour or its gravity [1].
The use of AI systems that create or expand facial recognition databases through the untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet or CCTV footage is prohibited [1].
The provided passages do not state when the ban on AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery applies.

The use of 'real-time' remote biometric identification systems in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement purposes for any of the objectives referred to in paragraph 1, first subparagraph, point (h) is restricted [2][3]. Such systems must be deployed only to confirm the identity of the specifically targeted individual [2][3]. The use must consider elements such as the seriousness, probability, and scale of harm or consequences for the rights and freedoms of all persons concerned [1][3]. Furthermore, the use must comply with necessary and proportionate safeguards and conditions under national law, including completing a fundamental rights impact assessment and registering the system in the EU database, unless there is a duly justified case of urgency [2]. Each use must also be notified to the relevant market surveillance authority and the national data protection authority [5].

In a duly justified situation of urgency, the use of a 'real-time' remote biometric identification system in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement may commence without an authorisation, provided that such authorisation is requested without undue delay, at the latest within 24 hours [1]. If the authorisation is rejected, the use must stop immediately, and all data, results, and outputs must be immediately discarded and deleted [1][2]. For post-remote biometric identification systems used in an investigation, the deployer must request authorisation, ex ante, or without undue delay and no later than 48 hours, unless it is for the initial identification of a potential suspect based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to the offence [4].

An AI system that manipulates material in a way that does not increase the exposure of any depicted intimate parts or alter the nature of any depicted sexually explicit activities shall not constitute manipulation [1b]. The prohibition under Article 5(1)(ba) applies to AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic images, videos, audio or similar material of an identifiable natural person’s intimate parts, or of an identifiable natural person engaged in sexually explicit activities, without the person’s freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent [2].

An AI system is considered high-risk if it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or if it is itself a product covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I, and the product requires a third-party conformity assessment for placing on the market or putting into service [1]. However, a product requiring a third-party conformity assessment solely due to risks other than risks to health and safety, such as risks relating to radio spectrum distribution or electromagnetic interference that do not affect health and safety, does not fulfill condition 1, point (b) [3]. Furthermore, AI systems listed in Annex III are also considered high-risk [4].

An AI system referred to in Annex III shall not be considered high-risk if it does not pose a significant risk of harm to the health, safety or fundamental rights of natural persons, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making [1]. This exception applies if the AI system is intended to perform a narrow procedural task [1]. It is also not considered high-risk if it is intended to improve the result of a previously completed human activity [1]. Furthermore, it is exempt if it is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review [1]. However, an AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk if it performs profiling of natural persons [1].

An AI system referred to in Annex III shall always be considered to be high-risk where the AI system performs profiling of natural persons [1]. If an AI system is intended to detect decision-making patterns or deviations from prior decision-making patterns and is not meant to replace or influence the previously completed human assessment, without proper human review, it may fall under a derogation from paragraph 2 [1]. However, the AI Act passages provided do not answer this question definitively regarding exam cheating.

AI systems intended to influence the outcome of an election or referendum or the voting behaviour of natural persons in the exercise of their vote in elections or referenda are listed as high-risk AI systems [1]. However, this definition explicitly excludes AI systems to the output of which natural persons are not directly exposed, such as tools used to organise, optimise or structure political campaigns from an administrative or logistical point of view [1].

Providers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, which is at least six months [1]. If the provider is a financial institution subject to Union financial services law requirements, they must maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept under that relevant financial services law [1].

Deployers of high-risk AI systems must keep automatically generated logs under their control for a period appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, for at least six months, unless Union or national law dictates otherwise [1]. If the deployers are financial institutions subject to Union financial services law requirements, they must maintain the logs as part of the documentation kept under that relevant financial service law [1].

In general, a report must be made immediately after the provider establishes a causal link or the reasonable likelihood of such a link, and no later than 15 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1]. However, in cases of a widespread infringement or a serious incident as defined in Article 3, point (49)(b), the report must be provided immediately, and no later than two days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of that incident [4]. If there is a death of a person, the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer has established, or as soon as it suspects, a causal relationship, but no later than 10 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [2].

If there is a death resulting from a high-risk AI system, the report must be provided immediately after the provider or deployer establishes, or as soon as they suspect, a causal relationship [1]. This report must be submitted no later than 10 days after the provider or deployer becomes aware of the serious incident [1].

Providers must ensure that AI systems designed to interact directly with natural persons inform those persons that they are interacting with an AI system [1]. This requirement is waived if the AI system is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute criminal offenses, provided appropriate safeguards are in place and the systems are available for public reporting of criminal offenses [1].

If you deploy an AI system that generates or manipulates a deep fake, you must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated [1]. This obligation does not apply if the use is authorized by law to detect, prevent, investigate, or prosecute a criminal offense [1]. If the content is part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional, or analogous work or program, the transparency obligations are limited to disclosing the existence of the generated or manipulated content in a manner that does not hinder the display or enjoyment of the work [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models must draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model, covering its training and testing process and evaluation results, for the AI Office and national competent authorities [2]. They must also put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, specifically to identify and comply with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [4]. Furthermore, providers shall draw up and make publicly available a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training the general-purpose AI model, using a template from the AI Office [5]. Providers must also draw up, keep up-to-date, and make available information and documentation to AI system providers, enabling them to understand the model's capabilities and limitations [1]. Finally, providers are required to cooperate with the Commission and national competent authorities in the exercise of their powers under the Regulation [3].

The Commission can consider the number of parameters of the model [3]. It can also take into account the quality or size of the data set, for example measured through tokens [2]. Furthermore, the criteria include the number of registered end-users [1]. The Commission may also consider the benchmarks and evaluations of capabilities of the model, such as its adaptability and level of autonomy [4]. Finally, the input and output modalities of the model are a criterion, including text to text, text to image, or multi-modality [5].
A general-purpose AI model is presumed to have a high impact on the internal market if it has been made available to at least 10 000 registered business users established in the Union [1].

Providers of general-purpose AI models must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights [1]. This policy must specifically address identifying and complying with a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 [1].

For SMEs, including start-ups, each fine referred to in Article 99 shall be up to the percentages or amount referred to in paragraphs 3, 4 and 5, whichever thereof is lower [1]. Member States must take into account the economic viability of SMEs, including start-ups, when imposing penalties [2].

An affected person who is subject to a decision made by a deployer based on the output from a high-risk AI system listed in Annex III, and which produces legal effects or significantly affects that person in a way they consider to have an adverse impact on their health, safety, or fundamental rights, has the right to obtain clear and meaningful explanations from the deployer [2]. This right applies to the role of the AI system in the decision-making procedure and the main elements of the decision taken [2]. However, this right will not apply if exceptions or restrictions follow from Union or national law in compliance with Union law [2]. Furthermore, this Article only applies to the extent that the right is not otherwise provided for under Union law [2].

Member States must ensure that their competent authorities establish at least one AI regulatory sandbox at the national level by 2 August 2027 [1]. This obligation can also be met by participating in an existing sandbox if that participation offers an equivalent level of national coverage for the participating Member States [1].

The passages state that for high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III, the provider must opt for one of several conformity assessment procedures when demonstrating compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2 [1][2][3][4][5]. These procedures depend on whether the provider has applied harmonised standards referred to in Article 40 or common specifications referred to in Article 41 [1][2][3][4][5].

For AI systems classified as high-risk AI systems related to products covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section B of Annex I, only Article 6(1), Article 60a and Articles 102 to 112 shall apply [1]. For high-risk AI systems related to products covered by Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I, only the derogations from the conformity assessment established in that Union harmonisation legislation shall apply [3].

The Regulation shall apply from 2 August 2026 [5]. However, certain parts apply from different dates [5]. For instance, Chapters I and II apply from 2 February 2025, with exceptions [5]. Chapter III Section 4, Chapter V, Chapter VII and Chapter XII and Article 78 apply from 2 August 2025, excluding Article 101 [5].

Operators of high-risk AI systems that were placed on the market or put into service before the date of application of Chapter III are only subject to the Regulation if those systems undergo significant changes in their designs as of that date [2]. Nevertheless, providers and deployers of high-risk AI systems intended for use by public authorities must take steps to comply with the Regulation's requirements and obligations by 2 August 2030 [2].

A 'deployer' is a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority, unless the AI system is used in a personal non-professional activity [1]. An 'operator' is defined as a provider, product manufacturer, deployer, authorised representative, importer or distributor [4].

For non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Article 5, the administrative fines for an undertaking can be up to EUR 35 000 000 or up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher [1]. For Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies, non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices referred to in Article 5 is subject to administrative fines of up to EUR 1 500 000 [2]. For non-compliance with any requirements or obligations under the Regulation other than those laid down in Article 5, the administrative fines for Union institutions, bodies, offices and agencies are up to EUR 750 000 [3].
